canberra.title: Awards roll in for Jerrabomberra mum keeping kids’ skin safe
canberra.snippet: A Canberra-born mum has won international acclaim for her sun safety invention to keep our children’s sensitive skin safe from the ...
canberra.content:
Anna-Lise Brink with daughter Daphne on the family holiday that inspired her business. Photo: Bebe Trek.

A Canberra-born mum has won international acclaim for her sun safety invention to keep our children’s sensitive skin safe from the sun.

Anna-Lise Brink first turned to a muslin wrap to keep her daughter Daphne safe from the sun on a family holiday to Far North Queensland.

But she told Region that she soon ran into problems.

She said her biggest shock was realising the cotton muslin wraps weren’t providing the coverage she thought they were.

“It’s awkward – they fly away. I was looking for something better and I couldn’t really find anything,” she said.

“But what I did discover was that muslin swaddles aren’t actually sun-safe. While they block some UV rays and they do provide shade, they don’t block enough UV rays to be considered sun protective.”

Ms Brink began developing an alternative by looking at what requirements sun-safe products met.

“Sunscreens have SPF ratings. Fabric has UPF ratings, and to be considered sun protective, fabric needs a minimum rating of UPF 15,” she said.

Ms Brink found muslin can have a UPF as low as five or six, and so began investigating other options.

What followed was 18 months of fabric testing, research, making prototypes and conducting breathability tests.

She launched her company Bebe Trek just over two years ago.

“I developed everything from my lounge room, my kitchen table, while I was on maternity leave,” she said.

The flagship product is a bamboo sun shade that features magnets and adjustable straps, and has a UPF 50+ rating.

“UV blankets do exist. They just don’t exist with magnets, apart from our product, and that took a regular item into something that becomes multifunctional, versatile.”

Ms Brink (pictured with daughter Penelope) founded Bebe Trek to make sure all parents can get out and about with their kids without “stressing about the elements”. Photo: Bebe Trek.

Ms Brink said that while they’d been building a strong customer base, she’d also received awards for her idea.

Bebe Trek recently took home four awards in the UK 2026 Organic and Sustainable Baby Awards, as well as two awards in the 2026 She-Com Women in E-Commerce Awards.

“It’s not an easy feat for a brand that’s just over two years old,” she said.

Ms Brink believes the products have been so well received for a simple reason.

“I think all parents just want to do what’s best for their babies and for the little ones,” she said.

“They always try to do the best with what they’re given … [This is a way to] make things easier for them – we’ve got the products to help them do that.”

Ms Brink said other Bebe Trek products were in development.

In recent weeks, she has launched “winter and rain” versions of the company’s main product.

“Getting outdoors with your baby isn’t always in summer. It’s not always going to be when it’s hot and it’s sunny,” she said.

“When it’s wet, when it’s cold, there are also times you want to get outdoors.”

Ms Brink thanked her family, who she said had been incredibly supportive as she balanced her company and a full-time role in the Australian Army.

“He’s now a full-time stay-at-home dad slash our warehouse manager,” she said of her husband.

“He’s the one who gets all the orders out to everyone, and then I run everything in the evenings after putting the kids to bed.”

Original Article published by Claire Sams on About Regional.

canberra.title: Conservation Council joins fight against proposed green waste facility site
canberra.snippet: The Conservation Council has bought into the debate over the proposed green waste facility in West Belconnen, linking it to the preservat...
canberra.content:
Brendan Trevaskis says the proposed green waste site on the other side of the trees would be a contamination risk. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The Conservation Council has bought into the debate over the proposed green waste facility in West Belconnen, linking it to the preservation of the ACT’s undeveloped Western Edge.

The council’s intervention comes as a petition gathers steam calling for the ACT Government to delay making a decision on permanently relocating the Parkwood Road green waste facility to Stockdill Drive and review all other potential sites.

The government has out for consultation Draft Plan Amendment 14, which would allow the proposed temporary site on Stockdill Drive to become permanent and add “recycling facility” and “bulk landscape supplies” to its uses.

An expansion of the site and creation of a new Resource Management Centre on the neighbouring block is also on the table.

Woolgrower Brendan Trevaskis fears the development of a major waste facility on his family property’s doorstep could result in contamination from run-off, spills into its creek and then the nearby Molonglo River, as well as dust and noise.

The City and Environment Directorate said mitigation measures such as leaching ponds and dams would be sufficient to prevent any contamination of waterways but Mr Trevaskis said the site was a steep slope and inappropriate for such a facility.

He said it had been sited on the steepest part of the block.

“They’re putting it in this one little narrow piece,” he said.

“They’ve got to go back and really look at it because I’ve had someone look at the grade of it and in the feasibility study they said it needed to be between one and eight grade and just going off ACTmapi, it’s showing a grade of nine.

“They’re just trying to push this one through and and not really looking at the big picture.”

Mr Trevaskis welcomed the input from the Conservation Council and the support from the petition.

West Belconnen residents along approach roads are also concerned about the impact of trucks heading to the facility.

The proposed Belconnen green waste site is on a steep slope. Image: Supplied.

Conservation Council executive director Simon Copland said the site was in the middle of ecologically sensitive land south of Drake Brockman Drive and east of Stockdill Drive.

He said it was a former vineyard that according to the Belconnen District Strategy 2023 was part of a blue-green ecological network of nature reserves connected by ecological corridors to the Molonglo River.

“It includes farms producing food and wool and forms a rural landscape backdrop which gives local residents, who live in the expanding suburban sprawl, access to scenic beauty and recreation,” Dr Copland said.

He said there would be heavy truck traffic and permanent composting with the risk of runoff, erosion and degradation of nearby waterways as a result of stockpiling and material handling.

“If this goes ahead, there is a risk of potentially harmful runoff down the natural drainage lines that flow southward toward the Molonglo River,” he said.

A Save our Western Edge protest at the ACT Legislative Assembly in March. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The council was particularly concerned that the proposed development was within the Western Edge, while the government claimed that it was still investigating the environmental values of the area.

“We are shocked that the ACT government is pushing forward with placing this suburban waste infrastructure in the Western Edge Investigation Area (WEIA), when it also says ‘there has been no government decision made as to whether any development will proceed in the WEIA’,” Dr Copland said.

“Even more concerning, the block is situated in Central Molonglo, which the government removed ‘in perpetuity from being considered as a future urban area’ in 2008.

“This is an area where farmers make a living and a haven for our slow-growing box-gum grassy woodland and iconic wildlife.”

Dr Copland said the 2022 Design Options Study made it clear that the recycling facility and bulk landscape supplies were just stage one in the ACT government’s plan to build a much larger Resource Management Centre, including landfill, perched right above the Molonglo River where runoff and rubbish could harm native fish, birdlife and platypus.

The council has recently released its new documentary On the Edge about the Western Edge which shares stories of the people working to protect it. The trailer can be seen here.

The Legislative Assembly petition sponsored by Liberal MLA Peter Cain said the proposal raised significant questions about environmental impacts, traffic, amenity, bushfire risk, odour, dust, noise, surrounding land uses and long-term strategic planning for North Canberra.

It questions the credibility and transparency of the planning process and calls for meaningful community consultation.

It also calls for a comprehensive review of all potential sites including on former CSIRO land acquired by the ACT Government and sites near Hall and that it be made publicly available.

It wants an independent community needs analysis to identify the current and future green waste collection and processing needs of Belconnen and the wider ACT and a final location selected for a new green waste facility in North Canberra.

DPA14 is open for consultation and written comments until 3 August.

canberra.title: Bigger space, bolder flavours mark 38 Katsu’s delicious evolution
canberra.snippet: What started as a popular stall at Verity Lane Market has grown into a permanent restaurant in the Canberra Centre, with 38 Katsu taking ...
canberra.content:
Managing director Jun Jang and chef Guno Chung are going big and bold at the new location. Photo: Sophia Brady.

What started as a popular stall at Verity Lane Market has grown into a permanent restaurant in the Canberra Centre, with 38 Katsu taking over the former Gami Chicken site on Bunda Street. For managing director Jun Jang and chef Guno Chung, the move marks the next step for a business that found a loyal Canberra audience almost from day one.

“Verity Lane was very successful for us. Canberra really embraced us, and we are so thankful for that,” said Jun.

“There was limited space there. Now we have a full restaurant, a cool room where we can age meat and do more experimental tasty things.”

The extra space has allowed them to evolve the menu and play with different ingredients and techniques. At the centre of it all, however, is the same philosophy that made the Verity Lane operation successful in the first place.

“38 Katsu is all about fast-paced casual food,” said Jun.

“Japanese comfort food is at the heart of what we do, sprinkled with Korean sensibilities that reflect our backgrounds, and we use Western influences picked up over years working in five-star establishments across Australia, Europe and the UAE.”

As you step off Bunda Street, the restaurant feels energetic and welcoming. K-pop and J-pop provide the soundtrack while a large mural stretches across one wall.

Jun explains it pays homage to the number 38 in their name; it references a traditional Japanese card game, and the sprawling artwork represents the full deck of cards. The fit-out itself is simple, with timber tables and QR ordering keeping the spotlight firmly on the food and fast service.

The menu is broader than the Verity Lane version, but one thing becomes obvious very quickly: pork is the main event here. That’s a smart move considering chicken is already well represented next door with Fricken.

To coax the maximum flavour out of the pork, chef Guno ages it in shio koji (a fermented rice and salt seasoning) for 48 hours before preparing it for katsu. The restaurant also uses wet panko crumbs, creating a coating that is noticeably different from your average breaded schnitzel. The result is a rustic crust built around the perfect crunch.

Beyond katsu, there are also soba, udon and yakisoba dishes, along with a selection of smaller bites. Photo: Sophia Brady.

There are plenty of other dishes competing for attention.

Doriya, a Japanese-style baked rice gratin topped with cheese and house-made white sauce, is not something I see often in Canberra, and it is available with seafood, chicken or vegetables. There are also udon, soba and yakisoba dishes, along with a selection of smaller bites.

I particularly like that every main arrives as a complete set on a tray with rice, miso soup, pickles and cabbage salad. Combined with the generous portions, it does feel like proper comfort food.

Around our table, we dive into the different cuts of pork, and there is a robust argument about whose dish is better and which cut is the superior option. The table is divided between the Rosu loin and the leaner Hire tenderloin.

Next, the debate moves to how katsu is best enjoyed: with curry or without curry? Everyone feels very passionately about their choices and is happy as a pig in mud with what they have in front of them.

The debate, however, becomes irrelevant when the 38 Signature Pork Katsu dish arrives.

38 Signature Pork Katsu dish is a showstopper. Photo: Sophia Brady.

The pork is thin, beautifully tender beneath a crisp golden coating, but what really makes the dish memorable is everything piled on top.

Shaved Parmigiano Reggiano sits over the cutlet alongside a rich house sauce that Jun jokes contains about 38 ingredients. It is a blend of bechamel and tonkatsu that forms a perfect gravy. Packed with savoury, salty and sweet goodness, it turns an already excellent pork katsu into a showstopper. It is also available with chicken katsu or cheese katsu.

If you like chicken parmi, this is its cooler, funkier (tastier!) Japanese cousin.

38 Katsu is located on the ground floor of the Canberra Centre at 148 Bunda St. They are open for lunch and dinner 7 days a week, and they will soon be serving Japanese beer, sake and a selection of wine to complement the food. Follow 38 Katsu on Instagram.

canberra.title: Melba youngsters peddle petition in bid to get bike track near home
canberra.snippet: Two young cyclists, who just want to ride their bikes and scooters on a safe, local pump track, have turned to people power for help. Sis...
canberra.content:
Sisters Celeste, six, and Edith, four Photo: Supplied.

Two young cyclists, who just want to ride their bikes and scooters on a safe, local pump track, have turned to people power for help.

Sisters Celeste, six, and Edith, four, both regularly travel around their home suburb of Melba with their bikes and scooters.

Unfortunately for the duo, the local bike park is too advanced for young riders to traverse safely.

So the girls took matters into their own hands and created a petition that has already gathered hundreds of signatures and captured the attention of MLA Chiaka Barry.

Their mother, Kate, said she was proud to see her kids take initiative and push for something they wanted, while also building community connection with other young riders in the Melba area.

“I’ve always taught my girls not to get angry about something they don’t have, but to get active about it, and so it’s really great to see them getting involved in this,” she said.

“They’ve been walking around the suburb, dropping flyers in letterboxes and really trying to get support.

“They’ve started taking it to school this week as well. Now that school’s back, we’ve really seen the numbers actually jump up in signatures of the petition.”

Eager cyclists Celeste and Edith are calling on Melba residents to support their push for a pump track in Melba. Photo: Supplied.

The petition, which is now active on the ACT Legislative Assembly website, needs 500 signatures to automatically trigger committee referral. As of writing, it is currently sitting just below 300.

“I first emailed Ms Barry about this opportunity; she was straight on the phone and supportive of it. So it did give us a really good momentum, just to know that there are people in Parliament who will support it,” Kate said.

“It actually puts a real smile on my face knowing that the kids really helped push this and possibly in the future, the kids would be using a park that they helped create.

“I think it’s so important for kids to understand that you can have the power to shape how things are and I think this is a really good lesson, not just for my kids, but for the whole community out here in Melba.”

The girls have been handing out posters they designed to help gain signatures for the track. The posters were hand-drawn and feature a QR code that links to the online petition.

“They’re coming home every day at the moment from school and asking how many signatures we’re up to,” Kate said.

“It’s just fantastic to see them so excited about it.

“They’re going to keep working to try and get more signatures and try and get the community involved.

“So many others have already joined in, which is just so great to see. We’re really hoping that we can get the signatures and show poor old West Belconnen some love.”

To sign Celeste and Edith’s petition for a new pump track in Melba, visit the ACT Legislative Assembly before 13 August.

canberra.title: Tilba Dairy in $1m move with the times, but some things don’t change
canberra.snippet: Tilba Dairy has secured a $1.1 million grant to increase production capacity and improve efficiencies so its premium products can be enjo...
canberra.content:
Tilba Dairy’s Jersey cows. Photos: Supplied.

Tilba Dairy has secured a $1.1 million grant to increase production capacity and improve efficiencies so its premium products can be enjoyed by its growing consumer base at competitive prices.

Owner-operator Erica Dibden said increasing the dairy’s production capacity meant it could buy more milk from local farmers, keeping that money local. With its products now reaching consumers in Canberra, Sydney and the Illawarra, Tilba Dairy’s “economic garden” is bringing more money back into the local economy, particularly if it sources as much as possible locally, while creating jobs.

The Tilba area has been renowned for its dairy products for more than a century. The dairy producers who remain have had to constantly change with the times. Throughout, Tilba Dairy has stayed true to its vision of producing quality food that is sustainable.

The $1.1 million funding through the NSW Government’s Agriculture Industries Innovation and Growth Program will enable it to continue to do that for years to come.

While Tilba Dairy has a high-speed, high-temperature continuous-flow pasteuriser that can process 15,000 litres of milk and milk for cheese production daily, it has only a small-batch pasteuriser for its cream and haloumi.

“We have to get the cream out by 11:30 am so we can get the haloumi in without everyone having to stay back late,” Ms Dibden said. “We need a bigger cream vat and a bigger haloumi vat.”

Tilba Dairy’s factory in Central Tilba.

Tilba Dairy produces up to 1000 tubs of cream at a time. Amazingly, once processed, the pouring into containers, putting on lids, labelling and dating tubs is all done by hand. Some of the grant will be spent on installing a cream and yoghurt filler similar to the filler it uses for milk.

Tilba Dairy’s factory is an old, inherited structure. It needs better maturing rooms for white mould cheeses such as brie and camembert.

Specialised ice-cream manufacturing is in Ms Dibden’s sights, but that is further down the track.

“We would love to do a Tilba Dairy ice-cream,” she said. “Our Jersey milk would be lovely for ice-cream.”

Despite cost-of-living pressures, demand for Tilba Dairy’s products continues to grow.

“That is testament to the product and testament to the consumers who support their local producers with low food miles,” Ms Dibden said.

She said if people did not support small food systems such as Tilba Dairy, there would be only big food systems; namely, completely automated factories where the product does not touch human hands and which are transported nationally. That would result in less competition, with consumers paying more for lower-quality products.

Tilba Dairy’s Trilogy cheese.

Tilba Dairy’s products are the result of fertile soil, beautiful Jersey cows, the plant and equipment associated with a dairy farm, and paying other local farmers a fair price for their milk.

“It is a very big investment and then there’s all the infrastructure at the shop, so it is absolutely expensive and that is reflected in our food costs,” Ms Dibden said.

To keep growing with the right balance of being an artisanal producer and commercially competitive, Tilba Dairy partners with other niche companies that have similar values of high-quality food that is sustainably produced.

“You can’t pay distributors 25 per cent and retailers want 40 per cent, but for us to grow we need retailers and distributors, so you have a synergy of things coming together,” Ms Dibden said.

Succession is a major issue for South Coast dairy farmers. It is a demanding job, making it a young person’s game, yet how many would have the millions of dollars to buy their own farm without family support. The Dibdens’ family farm has ceased operating but will continue to support local farmers by buying its milk from them to produce quality products it is proud to label Tilba Dairy.

“We hope to do some wonderful things and anchor Tilba’s future and viability for the years to come,” Ms Dibden said. “Purpose is part of what we do. Food production is feeding people. It has great purpose.”

Original Article published by Marion Williams on About Regional.

australia.title: Herbicide banned in 70 countries to be pulled from sale in Australia by chemical maker
australia.snippet: Syngenta says it will stop selling paraquat in Australia after new regulations on chemical linked to Parkinson’s disease Get our breaking...
australia.content:
Syngenta, the producer of a herbicide banned in more than 70 countries and which has been linked to Parkinson’s disease, will stop selling paraquat in Australia, saying new regulations has made it “commercially unviable”.

The decision to pull the product follows new restrictions on the highly poisonous chemical announced by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority in June.

Paraquat has been produced by the Swiss company for decades, but has long been linked to Parkinson’s disease in users.

It is banned in more than 70 countries and has been prohibited in the European Union since 2007.

It cannot be used in domestic settings in Australia, but is still widely used in agriculture, particularly broad-acre cropping like grains, sugarcane and cotton. The APVMA assessed that the weight of evidence does not show that paraquat exposure through approved uses increases the risk of developing Parkinson’s disease.

But it did impose new restrictions to address acute exposure and risks to animals.

The company said the decision to pull the products followed a commercial review carried out in the wake of the APVMA’s rules.

Syngenta ANZ’s managing director, David Van Ryswyk, said the company will manage the phase-out of its paraquat products in strict alignment with the APVMA’s designated sell-out and use-by timelines.

“Regulatory constraints, combined with a highly complex and increasingly expensive supply chain, have made the paraquat herbicide products commercially unviable,” Van Ryswyk said.

The new restrictions on the herbicide required that backpack sprayers be phased out, mandate additional personal protective equipment for users and set a much lower maximum rate of application per hectare.

At the time of the APVMA’s decision, Syngenta said the pesticide “does not cause an unacceptable environmental impact” and that the regulation would limit its use in a significant number of crop use cases.

The company had planned to continue supplying through a third-party manufacturer, but on Friday it said the new regulations and an increasingly expensive supply chain had made the product unviable.

Generic paraquat products will still be available for local farmers.

Last month, the Melbourne neurologist Associate Prof Wes Thevathasan told the ABC that there has been “global consensus” in his field that exposure to paraquat was linked to the development of Parkinson’s disease.

“There are now multiple epidemiological studies or real-world exposure studies that have suggested that paraquat increases the risk of Parkinson’s disease by around threefold,” Thevathasan said.

Grain Producers Australia spokesperson Andrew Weidemann said Syngenta’s decision created uncertainty for local growers.

“Its withdrawal leaves some important questions about what happens next,” he said.

“Australia is a relatively small market, and decisions like this call future investment into question.

“If companies cannot see sufficient value in maintaining products here, growers risk being left with fewer choices at the same time we urgently need more tools to manage herbicide resistance.”

australia.title: Lofty ambitions: can puffer jackets be made more sustainable?
australia.snippet: As temperatures dip, the puffer’s appeal inflates. But quality and filler are factors to consider before buying new Change by degrees off...
australia.content:
Whether you call it a parka, puffer or Tassie tuxedo, the insulated jacket has become a cold-weather closet staple.

A 1920s version by Australian mountaineer George Finch was constructed from hot air balloon fabric and eiderdown, but most modern designs are a mix of petroleum-based synthetics as well as animal and plant fibres, with varying environmental and ethical impacts.

Producing these materials, through agricultural or chemical processes, contributes 83% to the jacket’s overall carbon and water footprint, according to one life cycle study. The next largest contributor was water and energy usage during wear – with the average down jacket lasting seven years – followed by sewing and disposal. Natural fibres like down and wool also add animal welfare considerations.

But, like all clothing items, the effects are multiplied across global production and consumption systems. The market for puffers is large and growing, with more than 100m jackets made in China annually. Some brands are even branching into new territory, with demand for puppy puffers soaring.

Dr Carolina Quintero Rodriguez, a senior lecturer at RMIT University’s school of fashion and textiles, says advertising and social media are encouraging us to purchase more than we need.

“That is incentivising or creating a need in the population for not only one jacket, but you need three jackets,” she says.

A recent Adelaide University study of nearly 600 people’s clothing habits found 89% of garments are bought new, with padded jackets one of the most expensive items that people own, but rarely wear, which provides a ready supply of secondhand puffers in great condition. That’s why it’s important to choose a good quality garment, from a responsible brand, and wear it and repair it for as long as possible.

One jacket, many ingredients

Julie Boulton, a sustainable fashion consultant, says puffers usually consist of an inner and outer shell, a filler (“the stuff that makes it puff”), and notions like zips, snaps or buttons and thread.

Shells are usually made from fossil fuel-derived materials, such as nylon or polyester, sometimes blended with cotton or wool.

Jackets labelled “100% recycled” usually comprise polyesters made from plastic waste, such as water bottles or used textiles.

The padding inside often consists of duck or goose feathers (called down), wool, or a synthetic fill, Boulton says. Some brands, like Pangaia, are moving to plant-based fluff, made from wildflowers, biopolymers and aerogel.

According to the life cycle study, polyester fibre production, spinning, weaving, fabric dyeing and finishing are all high-energy consumption processes.

Polyester is a petroleum-based fibre that has issues with greenhouse gas emissions and shedding microplastics, Quintero Rodriguez says. Natural down is biodegradable and a byproduct of the meat industry, she says, but can come with risks associated with animal welfare and supply chain opacity.

Down is made by plucking the soft feathers of ducks or geese, usually after slaughter, according to the RSPCA, although a small percentage (1 to 2%) is still thought to be collected from live plucking, a practice the organisation says is a major welfare concern. Consumers are encouraged to look for the Responsible Down Standard, a voluntary certification that requires higher levels of animal welfare, traceability and prohibits live plucking.

When it comes to wool, Dr Natalie Roadknight, a senior scientific officer at the RSPCA, says the biggest welfare concern is a practice called mulesing, which involves cutting an area of skin near the tail. “It’s done while the lamb is completely conscious,” she says. “They’re able to feel the cuts”. Australia is one of the only countries where the practice is still legal, with the procedure banned in New Zealand and other countries.

Consumers can choose to avoid wool products that involve mulesing, by asking the brand directly, or looking for the ZQ Merino or the Responsible Wool Standard.

Re-wear and repair

Australians buy 1.5bn new items of clothing each year, and send 220,000 tonnes to landfill, a report by Seamless, Australia’s clothing stewardship scheme, has found.

“If you’re thinking about getting a jacket, look secondhand, look from your friends, don’t think that you’ve got to go and buy new,” says Boulton.

After that, the key is to keep it in service for as long as possible, she says. “While you’ve got it, use it, and wear it, wash it responsibly and take care of it and repair it.”

Some outdoor brands offer repair services or kits to help people patch and mend their winter coats. About one in 10 items are repaired, the Adelaide University study found, even though mending extended a garment’s useful life by 2.5 years on average.

Quintero Rodriguez says most garments don’t need to be washed as often as people think; sometimes, airing them out is enough. But if you do have to clean them, use cold water, she says, because heat can damage synthetic fabrics like nylons or elastane.

Gentle washing can also extend the life of water resistant or repellent surfaces in raincoats, with some finishes able to be reapplied or reactivated.

Can puffers be recycled?

Nationally, about half of unwanted clothes end up in landfill (53%), another 38% are reused locally or exported, and 9% are recycled.

Textile recycling is a time and labour intensive process, Boulton says, partly due to a lack of infrastructure and also because the price of virgin polyester is so cheap. Some outdoor brands do offer take back schemes, through places like Upparel.

“It’s cheaper just to make a whole new [jacket] than it is to recover and repurpose, or deconstruct, recycle and put back into the system again, which is such a shame.”

Quintero Rodriguez says: “My main message will be to extend the life of the item as much as possible. Care for the item as per the care instructions. And to make sure that you purchase [only] what you need.”

australia.title: Rebel Wilson had a legal win but didn’t come out of The Deb defamation trial unscathed
australia.snippet: Judgment dismissing Charlotte MacInnes’s case expressed doubts about credibility of three key witnesses, and is likely to be appealed Reb...
australia.content:
Rebel Wilson’s self-styled brand as a truth teller was put to the test during a fiery defamation feud where rivals called her a bully.

But the Hollywood A-lister, referred to as “very difficult to be around” and “fucking nuts” during an at-times bruising trial, emerged from the federal court battle with the last laugh.

The Pitch Perfect star came under fire while being sued by the Australian actor Charlotte MacInnes, who played the lead role in Wilson’s directorial debut film, The Deb.

MacInnes claimed she was defamed by Wilson in four social media posts implying she was a liar and a sellout who walked back a sexual harassment complaint to further her career.

Wilson wrote the young actor confided – and later recanted – she felt uncomfortable when the film’s co-producer Amanda Ghost asked to have a shower and a bath together.

MacInnes denied making a complaint, insisting she had not been uncomfortable when the pair shared a bath in their swimwear after Ghost suffered a medical episode in September 2023.

But in her ruling handed down on Wednesday, Justice Elizabeth Raper found evidence established MacInnes did make a complaint about feeling uncomfortable.

The young actor then walked it back, at least partially because she was concerned about losing control of the situation and wanted to contain it, the judge determined.

She ruled none of the four social media posts were defamatory in a comprehensive win for Wilson.

“This has been a long process and throughout I have tried to stay grounded in my values and what I believed was right,” Wilson wrote upon her victory. “I’m thankful that process has now reached its conclusion.”

Yet the Bridesmaids star did not escape the hotly contested trial without wounds.

For all Wilson’s protestations that she was known as a truth teller, Raper found the actor’s testimony had been untruthful on occasion, self-serving at times and punctuated with exaggeration.

MacInnes’s claims the first-time director would be believed because of her status in the entertainment industry were dismissed.

“It was my impression from all the evidence Ms Wilson is known for being outspoken but not necessarily reliable,” Raper wrote.

MacInnes faced the same scrutiny, with the judge finding she had been less than frank at times and combative when asked to accept reasonable suggestions.

She determined the young actor gave multiple inconsistent accounts of what happened in the Bondi apartment after the medical episode, as had Ghost.

“I have serious misgivings as to the truthfulness of the testimony of each of Ms MacInnes, Ms Ghost and Ms Wilson,” she wrote.

The scathing assessments may have MacInnes questioning why she sued her famous co-star.

But the defamation law expert Prof David Rolph said the case highlighted the risk of defamation litigation.

“People who sue for defamation or become involved in defamation cases don’t know and can’t control what’s going to come out in court,” the University of Sydney law professor said. “Once you start, it’s difficult to control and it’s difficult to stop what may be said about you in court.”

That became abundantly clear for Wilson, who was labelled a bully and a liar during the weeks-long hearing.

The Deb director denied the claims, labelling accusations of private and public bullying as nonsense and insisting she had been a champion of women throughout her 25-year career.

Raper noted she maintained her composure while being repeatedly charged with lying and fabricating evidence during her two-day cross-examination.

The accusations included that Wilson lied about having no involvement in the creation of smear websites attacking Ghost as the “Indian Ghislaine Maxwell” and a sex trafficker.

Raper made no determination of the contentious websites that loomed large during the trial, nor MacInnes’s allegation that Wilson was involved in a hack that resulted in a nude photo of hers being leaked.

Ultimately, the judge found, even if one of the posts had been defamatory, she could not be satisfied MacInnes had shown that she suffered serious harm.

The four posts had been visible to Wilson’s 11 million followers for 24 hours.

“The ordinary reasonable reader would have scrolled through the post relatively quickly and his or her reaction would have been impressionistic and fleeting,” she said.

The threshold of serious harm is a relatively new requirement yet to be tested in the country’s highest court, Rolph noted.

“The courts haven’t yet worked out precisely how to approach this issue and what’s required of it,” he said.

“It wouldn’t surprise me if a ground of appeal is raised in relation to serious harm because of the novelty of the issues and the novelty of the law.”

MacInnes indicated her intention to appeal against the decision, which has left her holding a hefty bill for the costs incurred by Wilson during the legal fight.

Rolph suggested such a high-profile loss may have a chilling effect on others considering litigation.

With a possible appeal looming, neither Wilson nor MacInnes can be said to have escaped without a scratch.

The actors began their relationship full of mutual admiration, working together on a film that was to elevate both of their careers.

But ended it on opposite sides of a stale Sydney courtroom, slinging accusations of lying and greed.

As Wilson wrote in her affidavit to the court: “Unfortunately, what started as a dream has turned out to be a nightmare.”

australia.title: It took months for an LGBTQ+ arts pop-up to resurrect an old church – but just three days to shut it down
australia.snippet: Group behind Divine Playhouse considering legal challenge and discrimination complaint after religious protests turned venue into culture...
australia.content:
It takes months of love and care to make an empty building come alive, but only three days to tear it all down.

This week, the gothic signage and queer absurdist art commissioned for Divine Playhouse had to be removed and placed into storage, as volunteers whitewashed a vibrant mural that had been painted on its walls.

After sitting empty for a year, Sydney’s St John the Evangelist church – which was deconsecrated in the 1930s – had been resurrected as an LGBTQ+ inclusive arts space, opening on 8 July with a year-long permit.

For just three days, Divine Playhouse existed as intended, hosting an opening night party, a queer comedy night and a disco.

But a day after religious groups gathered outside to protest its opening and called on the New South Wales government to withdraw its $100,000 arts grant, the venue’s landlord ordered the promoters, Heaps Gay Events, to cease “engaging in offensive trade” or risk eviction before terminating their lease a few days later.

Heaps Gay had until 5pm on Friday to vacate, which gave them three days to clear a space that had been months in the making. Their lawyers, meanwhile, are exploring whether they can sue for damages and make a sex discrimination claim.

“It’s not just about Divine any more, it’s about censorship,” the promoter and founder of Heaps Gay, Kat Dopper, told Guardian Australia.

“If we were to walk away, these groups will just get stronger and more powerful and louder.

“We can’t allow that to happen.”

‘Offensive trade’: legal questions raised over eviction

Located in the heart of Sydney’s central business district, the former church has housed a children’s school and a theatre since being deconsecrated nearly 100 years ago. As Divine Playhouse, it was intended to be a safe and inclusive queer-friendly arts space, organisers said.

At its opening night party, titled the First Rite, hundreds gathered for performances from drag artist Etcetera Etcetera, a DJ set by Stereogamous, performances from the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence, and a speech from the city’s deputy lord mayor, Jess Miller, who spoke of the “intergenerational magic” of spaces like this.

From the stage, Dopper announced the venue had changed its name from Unholy Playhouse at the last minute, answering concerns raised by people from the Christian community.

But Christian groups, including Fit for the Kingdom and the Prodigal Sons, still gathered to protest, taking issue with what a spokesperson from Fit for the Kingdom described as “hateful blasphemy that mocks what we hold most sacred”.

They pointed to social media images from the First Rite, featuring drag queens dressed as nuns, an attender wearing a corpus from a crucifix on a leather choker, and a performer in a pig costume offering french fries as holy communion.

A day after that party, lawyers acting for the landlord sent a notice of breach to Divine Playhouse, claiming its “offensive trade has caused … grievance and disturbance”; “offensive trade” was later cited as grounds for the eviction under section 129 of the Conveyancing Act 1919 (NSW).

The building is owned by developer Redevelop, founded by billionaires Anthony El-Hazouri and Charbel Hazzouri.

The landlords and their lawyers did not respond to repeated requests for comment, but told the Sydney Morning Herald they were not aware of how the space would be used and said it was “equivalent to hate speech” because it targeted people’s religious views.

“The events … they were targeting Christian beliefs … and, for us, it’s the height of offence to say it’s about arts and culture when you’re derogating an entire group’s belief,” El-Hazouri told the Sydney Morning Herald.

But the law firm representing Heaps Gay, Marque Lawyers, argues they did not have a proper basis for termination.

The notion of “offensive trade” finds its roots in 1840s English law and was historically used to regulate things like noxious smells, the managing partner of Marque Lawyers, Michael Bradley, said.

Its definition in the Conveyancing Act says lessees must not use, exercise, or permit “any noxious, noisome, or offensive art, trade, business occupation, or calling”.

“It’s never been applied to moral offensiveness in the way the landlord is seeking to do,” Bradley said. “We don’t doubt that the landlord is offended by what Heaps Gay was doing, but that’s a subjective personal question.”

Cathy Sherry, a Macquarie University professor and land law expert, said there was a “very strong possibility” that the definition referred to things that were physically offensive, as “noisome” and “noxious” were physical descriptors.

Allowing a landlord to define “offensive” to include what they found “morally offensive” could also pave the way for Australian property law to become more like the US, where restrictive covenants were used by developers to facilitate racial segregation and discrimination, she said.

“If one landlord can evict a tenant because they claim what they’re doing on the premises is offensive, then every landlord can.”

In a statement to the Guardian, Catholic group Fit for the Kingdom said nobody had stopped Divine Playhouse’s organisers from publishing, fundraising, speaking or performing, but that they welcomed the landlord’s decision to “refuse to allow their premises to host hateful content”.

“The prayer vigils [outside the venue] were always for prayer and public awareness of the issue: the targeted ridicule of our Catholic faith,” a spokesperson said.

“We don’t suggest the organisers or performers are less deserving of human dignity or safety, or target them as individuals.”

‘I’m so sad no one’s going to get to see the space’

Before they were evicted, Divine Playhouse had already made hundreds of bookings and was set to support more than 1500 artists, producers, performers, technicians, small creative businesses and staff during its year-long lease, organisers said.

Should the church’s landlords be found in breach of contract, Heaps Gay could claim substantial damages.

Lawyers are also examining whether the venue can make a complaint to the Australian Human Rights Commission, which could conduct conciliation to try to resolve the dispute.

If the complaint is not resolved, Heaps Gay could take the matter to the federal court.

While the legal options are being considered, Divine Playhouse is busy looking for a new home.

More than 18,000 people have signed a petition to back the venue and $41,000 has been raised to help cover artist fees, pay for lawyers and fund its move.

“I’m so sad that no one’s going to get to see the space,” Dopper said.

“It was such a nugget: it could have a stage in the round for bands, it could be a cabaret with the long catwalks and theatre … It was literally perfect.”

For days, volunteers and stakeholders have been flowing in and out of the building, rolling out speakers and putting commissioned artwork into storage.

But Keekee James’s mural, painted on to the walls of the building, can’t be packed away.

“It does feel like our version of blasphemy to paint it over,” Cecily Hardy, a Divine Playhouse representative, said. “Art throughout the ages has been censored, and this is our local version of that.”

Dopper maintained organisers were not mocking the church, and said they had responded to community concerns, including by adjusting its program.

Regardless of intentions, the NSW Council for Civil Liberties president, Tim Roberts, said Australians should be able to make fun of powerful institutions.

“If we cannot even mock a religion, that’s a silencing of our speech and discourse,” he said.

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, previously said it was “hard to believe that this is the best location for that kind of event”, while other Labor MPs including the NSW arts minister, John Graham, and Stephen Lawrence have since backed Divine Playhouse.

“[Christians] have the right to feel offended and to express that publicly,” said Lawrence, who is gay and was raised Catholic. “But we should jealously guard the right to artistic freedom and the way state grants accommodate that.”

Dopper is organising a fundraiser show for cancelled artists and a protest, which will be held on Saturday.

world.title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying
world.snippet: The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year Two Russian men have...
world.content:
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.

Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.

From 28-30 July 2025, a minibus taxi strike over fuel price hikes descended into riots and looting, in which 22 people were killed and more than 1,600 arrested according to official figures.

Angola’s security forces were accused of firing live ammunition at protesters; the government said its “progressive” use of force was justified. Human Rights Watch had previously said Angola employed “excessive force” when it used rubber bullets and teargas to break up a peaceful protest against rising fuel prices on 12 July 2025.

Angolan prosecutors said Lakshtanov and Ratchin wanted to influence next year’s presidential elections, including by funding Angola’s largest opposition party, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), or by forcing a leadership change within the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA), which has ruled the country since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Prosecutors also claimed the men were linked to Africa Politology, a Russian disinformation and propaganda network that emerged from the Wagner mercenary group.

Africa Politology was taken over by Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) after the death of the Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2023, according to an investigation by media outlets including Forbidden Stories. Wagner was rebranded as Africa Corps and absorbed by Russia’s military.

Angola, whose economy is highly dependent on oil exports, has historically been close with Russia. During the cold war years of Angola’s 1975-2002 civil war, the Soviet Union and Cuba supported the MPLA, while the US and apartheid South Africa backed its opponents, including UNITA. However, Angola’s president, João Lourenço, has improved relations with the US and Europe since taking power in 2017.

In the last decade, Russia has increased its presence in Africa. The Wagner group and then Africa Corps have provided security for the Central African Republic’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, since 2017.

In 2021, Wagner forces arrived in Mali to support the military junta. Africa Corps also backs the military regimes in neighbouring Niger and Burkina Faso. Since 2023, Russian troops have also been deployed in Equatorial Guinea, Libya and Sudan, according to a US Congress report.

Madagascar’s president, Michael Randrianirina, has also boosted ties with Russia since taking power in a coup in October 2025. There are Russians in his presidential guard and a weekly programme about Madagascar-Russia relations was launched earlier this month on national television.

Two Angolans were also tried alongside the Russians. The sports journalist Carlos Tomé received a two-year suspended prison sentence. Francisco de Oliveira, the secretary-general of UNITA’s youth wing, was acquitted.

Prosecutors have appealed against those sentences, according to the Portuguese news agency Lusa. Lakshtanov and Ratchin have also appealed against their sentences, but will remain in detention while the appeal is processed, according to Lusa.

Russia’s embassy in Angola did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Agence France-Press contributed to this report

world.title: MoD cancels army training in Kenya over powers to prosecute British soldiers
world.snippet: September exercise called off after Kenya raises concerns over funding and jurisdiction for criminal offences The British army has been f...
world.content:
The British army has been forced to cancel training for its troops in Kenya after the Kenyan government refused to ratify a bilateral defence agreement.

While the UK government wanted to renew the existing agreement, Kenyan lawmakers had sought changes to give local authorities greater powers to hold British soldiers accountable for any offences committed in the country.

According to the Kenyan news outlet the Daily Nation, the dispute centres on which cases Kenya will retain primary jurisdiction over, while the amount of money Britain pays Kenya to host the training camp has also been a sticking point.

The chair of the Kenyan national assembly’s defence, intelligence and foreign relations committee, Nelson Koech, said the two governments were “actively engaging to address these outstanding issues”.

As a result of the Kenyan government’s decision, a planned exercise involving the 1st Battalion the Duke of Lancaster’s Regiment, which was due to begin in September, has been cancelled.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “The UK highly values its relationship with Kenya, which is underpinned by mutual benefit, respect and cooperation. The UK-Kenya Defence Partnership is one of the great strengths of our relationship. Our joint training and operations with the Kenyan Defence Forces are keeping both Kenyan and British people safe.

“It is with regret that the necessary licences required to allow training to take place in Laikipia later this year have not been forthcoming. As a result, the planned training will now be conducted at an alternative location outside Kenya.”

Kenya also benefits from training of its own armed forces at BATUK, the British army base near Nanyuki, and the presence of British troops is valuable for the economy.

The MoD spokesperson added: “We recognise the disappointment this decision will cause for those who would have benefited from the economic activity generated by the exercise.”

They said the UK government remained “committed to our defence partnership with Kenya”, adding that the UK would “continue to engage closely with the Kenyan government to support the resumption of training in-country at the earliest appropriate opportunity”.

However, there has been sustained pressure from Kenyan people opposed to the British army’s continued presence. Last year, a report to the Kenyan parliament into the base alleged human rights violations, environmental destruction and sexual abuse by British soldiers.

The most high-profile case linked to the base is the death of Agnes Wanjiru, in which a British soldier has been charged with murder. Kenya has retained jurisdiction in the case and an extradition hearing is due to take place in November. Robert Purkiss denies the single charge of murder.

Legal proceedings had stalled since Wanjiru’s death in 2012, but advanced under John Healey’s tenure as defence secretary. As shadow defence secretary, he had called on the previous government to do more to progress the case.

Koech said the committee had called for “stronger accountability measures, including jurisdiction over serious offences, enhanced protection for local communities, and implementation of recommendations arising from the BATUK inquiry”.

world.title: Health worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital after working in DRC
world.snippet: UK resident was evacuated from Democratic Republic of the Congo where there is an outbreak of the disease A humanitarian worker is being ...
world.content:
A humanitarian worker is being monitored at a specialist hospital in London after potential exposure to the Ebola virus.

The UK resident was medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) where the worker had been treating patients with the disease, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.

UKHSA said the person was evacuated as a “highly precautionary measure”, adding: “The individual is not currently displaying any symptoms and remains well, but as a precautionary measure they have been evacuated on a flight chartered solely for the evacuation.

“They are now being assessed and monitored in isolation by infectious disease specialists at a London hospital.”

The agency said the incubation period of Ebola ranges from two to 21 days and the individual will be closely monitored and is required to isolate throughout this period.

There are no confirmed cases of Ebola in the UK and the risk to the general public remains low.

Richard Pebody, the director of epidemic and emerging infections at the UKHSA, said: “This individual has been transferred out of an abundance of caution and we’re pleased they remain well.”

Last month, a patient suspected of having the Ebola virus at a Glasgow hospital tested negative.

Precautionary measures were taken after the patient was admitted to the Queen Elizabeth University hospital.

An outbreak of the disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda in May was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the World Health Organization (WHO).

The virus is transmitted to people from wild animals and then spreads in the human population through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs or other bodily fluids of infected people and with contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding or clothing.

According to WHO, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle, pain, headache and sore throat. These are followed by vomiting, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, rash, and symptoms of impaired kidney and liver functions.

world.title: Healthy diet too expensive for one in three people globally, UN report finds
world.snippet: Global hunger declined for the third year in a row in 2025 but experts call for action to bring down costs of fruit, vegetables and dairy...
world.content:
One in three people cannot afford to eat a healthy diet, a new report has found, prompting calls for urgent action on food affordability.

There are 2.69 billion people unable to afford a diverse diet that meets their energy and nutrient needs, and it will take “immense” amounts of work to achieve the global target of zero hunger by 2030, the annual report from five UN agencies warned.

Global hunger declined for a third consecutive year in 2025, with 7.8% of people affected, down from 8.1% in 2024. There were also signs that a prolonged upward trend in Africa was coming to a halt.

However, the proportion of people who cannot afford a healthy diet remains “extremely high”, said Maximo Torero, chief economist of the Food and Agriculture Organization, one of the report’s authors.

The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2026 report calculated the cost of a healthy diet is 4.28 purchasing power parity (PPP) dollars a day. This means that in any given country, a healthy diet costs the amount of local currency with the same buying power that $4.28 has in the US.

“The extreme poverty line is $3PPP per person,” Torero said. “So it’s significantly higher.”

He said government policies had typically focused on subsidising cereals and starchy staples, rather than meat, dairy, fruit and vegetables.

“That means calories, but not a diversity of diet,” he said, highlighting the impact of this on rates of obesity and diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Figures from the World Health Organization, another of the UN agencies behind the report, show adult obesity rose from 12.1% in 2012 to 16.2% in 2024.

“It’s extremely urgent,” Torero said. “Obesity [among adults] is growing at a very steep level, so we need to now work intensively on trying to minimise those risks and those hidden costs that that substantial increase in obesity will bring.”

He called for investment in infrastructure, research and development. Modelling in the report suggests more efficient supply chains could bring down the costs of meat and dairy as well as fruit and vegetables. New policies to encourage greater consumption of fruit and vegetables could also pay dividends, he suggested, reducing the economic impact of health issues linked to poor diets.

In Africa, 66.6% of the population was unable to afford a healthy diet in 2025, more than double the levels observed in Asia or Latin America and the Caribbean.

Africa is now home to the highest number of hungry people for the first time, with about 309 million, surpassing Asia’s 292 million, the report showed.

The rise is largely driven by higher population growth on the continent, Torero said, with the proportion of the population going hungry actually starting to decrease “for the first time in years”.

“I think this is extremely important, because the numbers are for 2025, where already we have seen a significant reduction in overseas development assistance in the region,” Torero said.

Shipping restrictions in the strait of Hormuz linked to the conflict in the Middle East are likely to hit next year’s figures, he said.

The report is authored by the FAO, WHO, Unicef, the UN World Food Programme and the International Fund for Agricultural Development.

world.title: São Tomé and Príncipe heads to polls in tense presidential election
world.snippet: Incumbent Carlos Vila Nova hopes to defeat his former party and secure second term as independent Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to t...
world.content:
Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to the polls for a presidential election on Sunday as one of Africa’s least populous countries seeks to burnish its democratic credentials.

According to the National Election Commission, about 142,000 people are registered to vote in the tiny African state’s elections, approximately 15% of whom live in the diaspora.

Since gaining independence from Portugal in 1975, the island country off Africa’s west coast has built a solid reputation for peaceful, competitive elections. But this year’s vote comes amid a tense political atmosphere and a lingering constitutional crisis.

The president, Carlos Vila Nova, is running for a second term as an independent, rather than as the candidate for the ruling Acção Democrática Independente (ADI), whom he represented when he was elected in 2021.

The tensions between Vila Nova and his former party began in January last year when he dismissed the prime minister, Patrice Trovoada. Trovoada’s replacement, the former justice minister Ilza Amado Vaz, resigned after just three days, before the current holder, Américo Ramos, took office.

On Sunday, Vila Nova will be running against four other candidates including the ADI parliamentary leader, Nito D’Abreu. Another former prime minister, Jorge Bom Jesus, attempted to withdraw his independent candidacy, but missed the deadline and remains on the ballot.

The main opposition party, the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe, is now part of a broad coalition backing the incumbent president, despite being staunch ADI opponents. Meanwhile, an ADI faction led by Ramos is backing D’Abreu. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the election will go on to a second round.

The businessman Domingos Monteiro, known as “Nino”, who has been president of the São Toméan Football Federation since 2015, was disqualified after the constitutional court ruled he did not meet the eligibility requirements. Monteiro was born on the island, but his parents never became naturalised citizens after moving from Cape Verde where they were born.

“The constitutional court is violating the principle of equal rights … It is time for descendants born in São Tomé and Príncipe to say no to discrimination, to the culture of xenophobia and persecution,” said Monteiro.

For voters, priorities include tackling government corruption, high inflation, severe youth unemployment, chronic fuel shortages, and frequent blackouts. Rivals of Vila Nova are hoping this will keep him from a second term and propel them to the presidency.

Corruption in São Tomé and Príncipe “is the greatest catastrophe the country has experienced in this half-century [of independence”, D’Abreu said at the presidential debate on Tuesday.

The country is seen as a trusted western ally for security and maritime trade in the Gulf of Guinea, one of the world’s biggest maritime piracy hotspots. It also has offshore oil deposits that make a significant contribution to its economy. Observer missions from the European Union, G7+ and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries are on the ground to monitor the polls.
